did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens by describing a "fountain" that will be opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and impurity—that is, for purification and the removal of defilement.

Did you know? On that day, idolatry will be completely abolished: the names of the idols will be cut off from the land and never remembered again. The spirit of impurity will disappear along with them.
Did you know? Anyone who continues to prophesy falsely will be considered so dangerous that even his father and mother will demand his death, claiming that he spoke falsely in the name of the LORD.
Did you know? The prophets themselves will be ashamed of their visions and will no longer wear a hairy garment—the clothing associated in this chapter with presenting themselves as prophets.

Did you know? One of those who denies being a prophet presents himself as a farmer and even says that another man acquired him in his youth—a description that emphasizes his concealment of his former identity.

Did you know? When the man is asked about the wounds between his hands, he replies, "These are the wounds I received in the house of my friends." The verse presents his answer as part of his denial of being a prophet.
Did you know? In this verse, the shepherd is described as the LORD's "fellow man"—an expression emphasizing the leader's special status. When the shepherd is struck, the flock is scattered.
Did you know? The chapter describes a devastating division in the land: two-thirds will be cut off and perish, while the remaining third will be left in it.

Did you know? The surviving third will undergo testing and refinement in the fire, like silver being purified and gold being tested. Afterward, the people will call on the name of the LORD, and the LORD will say of them, "They are my people."
